pos: n. (John Downame, c. 1571–1652, London minister, author of The Christian Warfare)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; English Downame, of Downham, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: John Downame spent his ministry in London, latterly as rector of All Hallows the Great, and he wrote two of the largest works of English practical divinity: The Christian Warfare, in four parts, on the believer's conflict with Satan, the world and the flesh, and A Guide to Godlynesse, a vast directory of Christian duty. He was also one of the licensers of divinity books in London and had a hand in the Westminster Annotations. His analysis of temptation is detailed to a degree the modern reader finds exhausting: he catalogues the devil's methods, the believer's excuses, the occasions of relapse, and the particular comforts for each case. The dictionary values precisely that patience. A generalised exhortation to resist sin helps nobody; what helps is a minister who has thought about the specific way a specific temptation works on a specific sort of person, and who has the armour of God ready to name piece by piece.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines warfare as military service and contest, and temptation as enticement to evil by arguments or by the offer of some good.
webster_full: W'ARFARE, n. Military service; military life; war; contest; struggle for victory.
TEMPTA'TION, n. The act of tempting; enticement to evil by arguments, by flattery, or by the offer of some good or apparent good.
AR'MOUR, n. Defensive arms; any habit worn to protect the body in battle.
DIREC'TORY, n. A rule to direct; a book containing directions.
scriptures: Eph 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Eph 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
Eph 6:13
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
corruption_summary: His Christian Warfare anatomised temptation in detail, so that the armour of God could be named piece by piece.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern preference for a short word on sanctification: a principle, a slogan, a single posture, applied to every case. Downame assumed that the adversary works by particular devices on particular men and that a minister owes his people particular answers. That is why his books are long, and it is why they were used.

The principle to recover is that the conflict is real, the enemy is personal and intelligent, and the equipment is given. “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Eph 6:11). The opposition is not merely internal: “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers” (Eph 6:12). The posture required is watchfulness: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about” (1Pe 5:8). And the end of the whole equipment is simply to be left standing — “and having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13).

“and having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13) — a Guide to Godlynesse for ordinary duty.

pos: n. (George Downame, c. 1563–1634, Calvinist Bishop of Derry and controversialist on justification)
etymology: Greek Georgios, a husbandman; English Downame, of Downham, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: George Downame, elder brother of John, was professor of logic at Cambridge, a leading English exponent of the Ramist method, and from 1616 Bishop of Derry in the Church of Ireland. He wrote a substantial treatise on justification against Cardinal Bellarmine and the Roman doctrine of inherent righteousness, and he preached and published on the covenant of grace. The dictionary names him to make a point the English story often obscures: in the generation before Laud, a man could be a bishop and a thorough Calvinist, holding unconditional election, particular redemption and imputed righteousness, and be thought no anomaly. The later alignment of episcopacy with Arminian and ceremonial religion was a change, not an inheritance. Downame's own diocese in Ulster was the one place where a Calvinist episcopate and a largely Scottish Presbyterian ministry worked side by side for a generation, until Wentworth and Bramhall ended the arrangement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inherent as existing in something else so as to be inseparable, and imputed as attributed or charged to one.
webster_full: INHE'RENT, a. Existing in something else, so as to be inseparable from it; innate; naturally pertaining to.
IMPU'TED, pp. Charged to one; attributed; ascribed; set to the account of another.
EPIS'COPACY, n. Government of the church by bishops; that form of ecclesiastical government in which diocesan bishops are established.
LOG'IC, n. The art of thinking and reasoning justly.
scriptures: Rom 4:6
Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,
Phi 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Isa 64:6
But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away.
Jer 23:6
In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely: and this is his name whereby he shall be called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS.
corruption_summary: A thorough Calvinist bishop who wrote against Bellarmine on inherent righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is the Roman doctrine of justification by an inherent righteousness: that God makes a man righteous by infusing grace into him, so that he is finally accepted on the ground of a righteousness now his own, increased by cooperation and lost by mortal sin. Downame answered it with the Reformed distinction — the righteousness that justifies is Christ's, reckoned to the believer and received by faith alone; the righteousness that sanctifies is worked in him by the Spirit and is never the ground of his acceptance.

The standard is Paul's account of his own case. He desires to be found “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ” (Phi 3:9). The reckoning is explicit: God “imputeth righteousness without works” (Rom 4:6). What our own best righteousness is worth as a ground is stated without flattery: “all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags” (Isa 64:6). And the name of the promised King is the whole answer — “THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS” (Jer 23:6).

pos: n. (Daniel Dyke, d. 1614, Puritan preacher, author of The Mystery of Selfe-Deceiving)
etymology: Hebrew Daniyyel, God is my judge; English Dyke, dweller by the ditch or embankment.
biblical_def: Daniel Dyke was a Cambridge man, suspended for refusing the subscription demanded of him, and chaplain to the Lady Harington; he died young and his brother Jeremiah published his papers. The chief of them is The Mystery of Selfe-Deceiving, an extended treatment of Jeremiah's verse on the deceitfulness of the heart, which traces the ways a man misreads his own case: counting intentions as obedience, mistaking natural temper for grace, grading himself against worse men, repenting of consequences rather than of sin. It was translated into French and read across Europe. The dictionary reckons it one of the indispensable Puritan books, and notes what distinguishes it from its modern imitations. Dyke is not teaching introspection as a practice; he is warning that the heart lies, and sending the reader outside himself — to Scripture, which judges him, and to Christ, who saves him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines self-deceit as the deceiving of one's self, and hypocrisy as a feigning to be what one is not.
webster_full: SELF-DECEIT', n. The deception of one's self respecting one's character or condition.
HYPOC'RISY, n. Simulation; a feigning to be what one is not; a false appearance of virtue or religion.
DECEIT'FUL, a. Full of deceit; trickish; fraudulent; tending to mislead.
INTROSPEC'TION, n. A view of the inside or interior; a looking inward.
scriptures: Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
Gal 6:3
For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.
Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults.
corruption_summary: His Mystery of Selfe-Deceiving traces how a man misreads his own case, and sends him outside himself for the remedy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the therapeutic turn inward that Dyke's title can be made to sound like and is not. Modern self-examination is usually offered as a path to self-knowledge and thence to self-acceptance, with the self as both investigator and judge. Dyke's whole premise is that this cannot work, because the investigator is the liar; the examination he teaches is conducted by the word of God on a man who has already despaired of his own verdict.

The principle to recover is that the heart is not a reliable witness about itself and God is. “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jer 17:9). Denial is itself the first deception: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1Jo 1:8). Self-importance is listed as self-deceit: “if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself” (Gal 6:3). And the only safe conclusion is the psalmist's request — “Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults” (Psa 19:12).

Hebrew anash (H605) — sick, incurable, desperately wicked; Jeremiah 17:9.

Greek phrenapatao (G5422) — to deceive one's own mind; Galatians 6:3.
Hebrew sether (H5643) — a covering, a secret place; Psalm 19:12.

“we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1Jo 1:8) — intentions counted as obedience.
“cleanse thou me from secret faults” (Psa 19:12) — examination conducted by the word, not the self.

pos: n. (Nicholas Byfield, 1579–1622, preacher at Chester and Isleworth, expositor of Colossians and First Peter)
etymology: Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; English Byfield, dweller by the field.
biblical_def: Nicholas Byfield preached at Chester and then at Isleworth, and left long expositions of Colossians and of the first epistle of Peter, together with a catechetical work and a treatise on the signs of a true believer. He preached and wrote through years of agonising illness — the stone that killed him at forty-three was reported to weigh some thirty-three ounces — and his commentaries were produced from the pulpit, lecture by lecture, in that condition. The dictionary names the method as much as the man. Byfield worked through an epistle verse by verse over years, so that his congregation received the whole of Peter or the whole of Colossians rather than a selection of favourite texts, and the printed volumes are simply the sermons. Continuous exposition of whole books is the plainest way a congregation gets the balance of Scripture instead of its minister's preferences.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exposition as the act of laying open the sense, and lecture as a discourse read or pronounced on any subject.
webster_full: EXPOSI'TION, n. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of an author.
LEC'TURE, n. A discourse written or pronounced on any subject; a discourse on the Scriptures.
EPIS'TLE, n. A writing communicated from one person to another; one of the letters of the apostles.
SE'RIES, n. A continued succession of things in the same order; a course.
scriptures: As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: He expounded whole epistles lecture by lecture through years of agonising illness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is topical preaching as a settled diet. A minister who chooses his own texts week by week will, without intending it, preach his own emphases, avoid what he finds difficult, and never reach the passages his people most need; and the congregation will never know what it has not heard.

The principle to recover is that a church is to be given the whole counsel of God and fed what makes it grow. “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — which required three years of night and day labour: “by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears” (Act 20:31). The diet is the word itself: “As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1Pe 2:2). And the charge is to preach it in season and out — “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

“be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — years of it under a mortal illness.

pos: n. (Ezekiel Culverwell, c. 1554–1631, Puritan minister, author of A Treatise of Faith)
etymology: Hebrew Yechezqel, God strengthens; English Culverwell, the dove's spring or well.
biblical_def: Ezekiel Culverwell ministered at Great Stambridge in Essex, where Thomas Hooker was converted under his preaching and John Winthrop sat under it; he was suspended for nonconformity and spent his later years in London writing. His Treatise of Faith is a careful answer to a question the Puritan ministry was constantly asked: how a man may know he truly believes. Culverwell's answer avoided the two errors on either side — he would not let a man rest in a bare profession, and he would not make assurance so difficult that only the extraordinary Christian could have it. He directed the doubting to the promise and to the Spirit's witness rather than to the strength of their own feelings. The dictionary names him for that pastoral balance, and for the men his pulpit sent out: the Essex congregations he served supplied a notable share of the ministers and magistrates who founded New England.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assurance as firm persuasion and full confidence, and promise as a declaration which binds the person who makes it.
webster_full: ASSU'RANCE, n. Firm persuasion; full confidence or trust; freedom from doubt; certain expectation.
PROM'ISE, n. In a moral and legal sense, a declaration, written or verbal, which binds the person who makes it.
WIT'NESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence.
DOUBT, n. A fluctuation of mind respecting truth or propriety; uncertainty.
scriptures: Rom 8:16
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:
These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God.
Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall:
Heb 6:11
And we desire that every one of you do shew the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end:
corruption_summary: His Treatise of Faith answered how a man may know he believes, without bare profession or impossible standards.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse again lies on both sides. One is the easy assurance that rests on a remembered decision and never asks whether anything followed; the other is a morbid scrupulosity that makes certainty the reward of exceptional feeling, so that ordinary believers conclude they were never converted. Culverwell was answering real people in the second condition and would not comfort them with the first.

The principle to recover is that assurance is attainable, is grounded in the promise, and is confirmed by the Spirit and by obedience. “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God” (Rom 8:16). John wrote precisely so that believers might be certain: “that ye may know that ye have eternal life” (1Jo 5:13). Diligence is commanded toward it: “give diligence to make your calling and election sure” (2Pe 1:10). And the full assurance of hope is a thing to be pressed toward, not presumed — “the full assurance of hope unto the end” (Heb 6:11).

pos: n. (Nicholas Bownd, d. 1613, rector of Norton in Suffolk, author of The Doctrine of the Sabbath)
etymology: Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; English Bownd, a variant of Bound, a dweller at the boundary.
biblical_def: Nicholas Bownd was rector of Norton in Suffolk and the author of The Doctrine of the Sabbath, published in 1595 and enlarged in 1606, the book that gave English Puritanism its distinctive doctrine of the Lord's Day. Bownd argued that the fourth commandment is moral and perpetual, that its substance binds Christians, that the day has been changed by apostolic authority to the first of the week, and that the whole day belongs to public worship, private devotion and works of mercy. The book was attacked at once by the authorities and was enormously influential anyway; the English and Scottish sabbath of the following three centuries, and the American one, descend from it. The dictionary records that influence soberly. Bownd's doctrine was a recovery of a commandment that late medieval practice had buried under a calendar of holy days, and its later hardening into mere prohibition was not his doing, though his book supplied some of the material.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sabbath as a day of rest set apart for religious duties, and holy day as a day set apart for commemoration.
webster_full: SAB'BATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed as a day of rest; among Christians, the first day of the week.
HO'LY DAY, n. A day set apart for commemorating some important event; a festival.
PERPET'UAL, a. Never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; everlasting.
DEVO'TION, n. The state of being dedicated or consecrated; piety; religious worship.
scriptures: Exo 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:
Mar 2:28
Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath.
Act 20:7
And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight.
corruption_summary: His 1595 book gave English Puritanism its doctrine of the Lord's Day, and the English-speaking sabbath descends from it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption, common now even in churches that keep a Sunday, that the day's sanctity is a matter of custom. Bownd's argument was that it is a matter of commandment, and a commandment that stands in the middle of a table of moral law written by God's own finger, flanked by the prohibitions of murder and idolatry.

The principle to recover is the commandment itself and its intended character. “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8). It is to be honoured by turning from one's own pleasure and calling it a delight: “call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable” (Isa 58:13). Its Lord is Christ: “Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath” (Mar 2:28). And the apostolic practice on the changed day is recorded plainly — “And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them” (Act 20:7).

pos: n. (John Brinsley the elder, fl. 1581–1624, Puritan schoolmaster of Ashby-de-la-Zouch and author of the Ludus Literarius)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; English Brinsley, a place-name surname of Nottinghamshire.
biblical_def: John Brinsley the elder kept the grammar school at Ashby-de-la-Zouch and wrote the fullest account of English schoolmastering of his age: the Ludus Literarius, cast as a dialogue between two masters, on how to teach a boy to read, write, construe, keep a commonplace book and pray. He also published a scheme for teaching Latin by close double translation and a tract urging that schools be planted in Wales, Ireland and the Virginia colony. He was a Puritan and the brother-in-law of Joseph Hall, and he was eventually silenced. The dictionary names him because his subject is the one every reforming generation neglects. A Reformation that does not get into the schools lasts one generation, and Brinsley's book is the English Puritan answer to that: patient, technical, concerned with how a slow boy is actually taught, and theological at the root, since he held that a child is taught to read chiefly in order to read Scripture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grammar school as a school in which the learned languages are taught, and construe as to interpret or arrange words to discover the sense.
webster_full: GRAM'MAR SCHOOL, n. A school in which the learned languages are grammatically taught.
CON'STRUE, v.t. To arrange words in their natural order; to interpret; to explain.
COM'MONPLACE BOOK, n. A book in which things to be remembered are recorded under general heads.
SCHOOL'MASTER, n. The man who presides over and teaches a school.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Psa 78:6
That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children:
corruption_summary: His Ludus Literarius taught English masters how to teach, so that children could read Scripture for themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the separation of schooling from the faith that founded it, so that Christians who would never let a stranger preach to their children will let anyone teach them to read, write and reason. Brinsley took the opposite view: the method, the texts, the discipline and the prayers of a school are all part of the formation, and he wrote four hundred pages on the details.

The principle to recover is that children are to be taught deliberately, early and at home as well as at school. “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). The instruction is continuous: “And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way” (Deu 11:19). Timothy's case shows how early it begins and what it is for: “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation” (2Ti 3:15). And the object is a generation not yet born — “That the generation to come might know them” (Psa 78:6).

pos: n. (Samuel Ward, 1577–1640, town preacher of Ipswich, imprisoned for a print and for nonconformity)
etymology: Hebrew Shemuel, asked of God; English Ward, a watchman, a guard.
biblical_def: Samuel Ward was town preacher of Ipswich for some thirty years, a plain and witty pulpit man whose sermons on the woe of drunkenness and on the use of the tongue were often reprinted. He got into trouble twice. First for a satirical engraving he designed in 1621, setting the Spanish Armada, the Gunpowder Plot and the pope in one picture, at a moment when the crown was negotiating a Spanish marriage, for which the ambassador had him questioned and briefly imprisoned. Second and more seriously for refusing conformity to Laud's ceremonial requirements, for which he was suspended, imprisoned, and finally driven to the Netherlands, returning to die at Ipswich. The dictionary notes the distinction between the two cases. A preacher may be punished for political indiscretion and for faithfulness in the same career, and he should not confuse the first kind of suffering with the second; Ward's own later letters make it clear which he reckoned worth it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines satire as a discourse exposing the faults of a person or people, and conformity as compliance with the usages of an established church.
webster_full: SAT'IRE, n. A discourse or poem in which wickedness or folly is exposed with severity.
CONFORM'ITY, n. Correspondence with a model; compliance with the usages of the established church.
SUSPEN'SION, n. The act of debarring, for a time, from the execution of an office.
ENGRA'VING, n. The act or art of cutting figures on metal; a print taken from an engraved plate.

Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters.
Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: Imprisoned once for a political print and once for refusing Laud's ceremonies, and he knew the difference.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the collapsing of all opposition into persecution. A Christian who is criticised for a tactless remark, an ill-judged publication or a political enthusiasm is not thereby suffering for Christ, and the New Testament is careful about the distinction; treating every consequence of our own folly as a cross cheapens the word and makes the church look self-pitying.

The principle to recover is that the cause of the suffering determines its character. Peter draws the line: “But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters” (1Pe 4:15). The blessing attaches to the other case: “Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf” (1Pe 4:16). And our Lord specifies the ground — “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10) — while the rule when the two collide is unchanged: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

pos: n. (Robert Harris, 1581–1658, Westminster divine, President of Trinity College, Oxford, plain preacher)
etymology: Germanic Hrodberht, bright in fame; English Harris, son of Harry.
biblical_def: Robert Harris was vicar of Hanwell in Oxfordshire for some thirty years, a member of the Westminster Assembly, and from 1648 President of Trinity College, Oxford. He was celebrated in his own time for the plainness of his preaching: short sentences, homely comparisons drawn from farming and household work, doctrine stated and then applied in particulars, and no display of learning in the pulpit although he had plenty of it. His printed sermons read as though spoken. The dictionary names the style as a deliberate discipline rather than a lack. Plain preaching in that generation was a method, taught and defended — open the text, raise the doctrine, prove it, answer objections, apply it to the several conditions of the hearers — and its aim was that a ploughman and a fellow of a college should both go home knowing what the text said and what to do about it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plain as evident to the understanding, without ornament, and application as the act of applying doctrine to practice.
webster_full: PLAIN, a. Evident to the understanding; clear; manifest; not obscure; without ornament.
APPLICA'TION, n. The act of applying; the act of fixing the mind; in preaching, the use made of doctrine.
DOC'TRINE, n. Principle or position in any science; whatever is taught; a principle of religion.
SIMILITUDE, n. Likeness; resemblance; a comparison or simile.
scriptures: And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth.
corruption_summary: Thirty years of deliberately plain preaching, so that a ploughman and a fellow both went home knowing the text.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the confusion of plainness with shallowness, in both directions. A preacher may hide thin content behind homely illustration and call it accessibility; or he may mistake obscurity for depth and leave a congregation admiring what it did not follow. The Puritan plain style was neither: it was a structure for getting difficult doctrine completely into the heads of ordinary people.

The principle to recover is that intelligibility is a duty and that the power is not in the manner. “my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4). The handling of the word must be straight: “nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience” (2Co 4:2). Five understood words beat ten thousand unintelligible ones — “I had rather speak five words with my understanding” (1Co 14:19) — and the Preacher's own labour was to find words both acceptable and upright: “The preacher sought to find out acceptable words” (Ecc 12:10).

pos: n. (Samuel Crooke, 1575–1649, rector of Wrington in Somerset for forty-seven years)
etymology: Hebrew Shemuel, asked of God; English Crooke, dweller by the bend, or a maker of crooks.
biblical_def: Samuel Crooke was a fellow of Emmanuel College who in 1602 took the living of Wrington in Somerset and held it for forty-seven years until his death, declining better offers. He catechised the parish systematically, left a compendium of divinity drawn up as a table of the whole body of doctrine, and published sermons on the guide of a Christian's life; his funeral sermon was preached by a neighbouring minister who had known him for four decades. The dictionary ends the night's batches with him on purpose. Almost nothing happened to Samuel Crooke. He was not imprisoned, exiled, martyred, promoted or famous; he preached twice on Sunday and catechised in the week in one Somerset village for nearly half a century, and the village was different at the end of it. The Reformation that this night's hundred entries describe was carried, in the main, by men like that, and the records do not keep their names.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incumbent as one in present possession of a benefice, and catechise as to instruct by question and answer.
webster_full: INCUM'BENT, n. A person who is in present possession of a benefice or of any office.
CAT'ECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and receiving answers, and by correcting the answers.
LIV'ING, n. The benefice of a clergyman; an estate appropriated to the support of a minister.
COMPEN'DIUM, n. A brief compilation containing the principal heads of a larger work.
scriptures: Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
corruption_summary: Forty-seven years in one Somerset village, catechising; almost nothing happened to him, and the village changed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the appetite for a notable ministry, which teaches a young minister to measure his years by events and leaves him restless in the parish he actually has. The long, uneventful, catechetical pastorate is the form in which most real reformation of a people has happened, and it is almost invisible in the records because nothing about it is quotable.

The principle to recover is that faithfulness and not scale is what is required and what is commended. “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). The commendation at the end is not for magnitude: “Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Mat 25:21). The apostolic pattern is years of patient warning — “by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears” (Act 20:31) — and small beginnings are not to be despised: “who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10).
